title: Esau’s Embrace and Jacob’s Altar
summary: Jacob bows before Esau and is embraced instead of attacked, presses his gift as restitution, parts from his brother in peace, and raises an altar at Shechem.
historicalContext: Twenty years have passed since Jacob fled Beersheba under Esau’s threat of murder (27:41-45; 31:38, 41). Esau, now settled in Seir south of the Dead Sea, comes north with four hundred men, the size of a raiding band (32:6). The court manners of the second millennium explain much of the meeting: letters from Canaanite rulers to Pharaoh in the fourteenth century speak of falling at the king’s feet seven times, and a superior’s acceptance of a present signalled that he accepted the giver and would not harm him. Succoth lay in the Jordan Valley near the Jabbok, later within Gad (Joshua 13:27). Shechem, in the central hill country, was an old city where Abram had built his first altar in Canaan (12:6-7). The plot Jacob bought there later held Joseph’s bones (Joshua 24:32), and a well near it was still called Jacob’s when Jesus sat beside it (John 4:5-6).
literaryContext: Following directly on the night at Peniel, chapter 33 resolves the tension left by the stolen blessing of chapter 27. The two meetings are bound by the language of the face: Jacob hoped to see Esau’s face and be accepted (32:20), saw God face to face and lived (32:30), and now says that seeing Esau’s face is like seeing God’s (33:10). Words for grace, gift, and blessing run through the dialogue, and “my blessing” in verse 11 recalls the blessing taken by fraud (27:35-36). He calls himself servant and Esau lord, reversing Isaac’s words in 27:29, while Esau calls him brother. Five quick verbs of welcome in verse 4 answer the five blunt verbs with which Esau once despised his birthright (25:34). The brothers part, and Jacob’s arrival “in peace” at Shechem echoes his Bethel vow (28:21). The altar recalls Abram’s first altar, and the location prepares for the grief of chapter 34 and the summons to Bethel in chapter 35.
themes: God answering prayer by changing a brother’s heart
Humility and restitution after long estrangement
Grace received from God and sought from others
Seeing God’s mercy in a reconciled face
Peace between brothers who walk different roads
Return to the land and worship of the God of Israel

outline.title: The Brothers Meet
outline.summary: Jacob arranges his family, goes ahead bowing seven times, and Esau runs to embrace and kiss him as both men weep.

outline.title: Gift, Grace, and the Face of God
outline.summary: Jacob presents his family as God’s gracious gift, explains the droves, and urges Esau to accept his blessing, likening Esau’s welcome to seeing God’s face.

outline.title: Parting in Peace
outline.summary: Jacob declines Esau’s company and escort for the sake of his children and flocks; Esau returns to Seir and Jacob settles for a time at Succoth.

outline.title: Home in Canaan with an Altar
outline.summary: Jacob arrives safely at Shechem, buys the field where his tent stood, and raises an altar named for God, the God of Israel.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold, Esau came, and with him four hundred men. And he divided the children unto Leah, and unto Rachel, and unto the two handmaids.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The night of wrestling is over, the sun has risen on a limping man (32:31), and at once the threat he had dreaded comes into view. “Jacob lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold” is a Genesis formula that often introduces a turning point arranged by God: Abraham looked up and saw the ram (22:13), and Rebekah looked up and saw Isaac (24:63-64). The expression prepares the reader for more than danger. Still, what Jacob sees is alarming: “Esau came, and with him four hundred men.” The messengers had reported that number the day before (32:6), and nothing has yet explained it. Four hundred armed men was the size of a fighting force (1 Samuel 22:2; 30:10).

Jacob divides the children among their mothers. On the previous day he had split his whole company into two camps so that one might escape if the other were struck (32:7-8). Now he groups his household by family, Leah’s children with Leah, Rachel’s with Rachel, and the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah with their mothers. The arrangement prepares for a formal presentation to Esau, and it also keeps each mother responsible for her own little ones if something went wrong.

The verse holds two realities together. Jacob has just been blessed by God and given a new name, yet he still takes careful practical steps. Faith in Genesis does not cancel prudence. The prayer of 32:9-12 had asked God to deliver him from Esau’s hand, and the answer is about to arrive in a form Jacob had not imagined. He is walking toward it with his eyes open.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשָּׂא … עֵינָיו וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה (vayyissa … ‘enav vayyar vehinneh) — lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold
wordNotes.explanation: A recurring narrative phrase that slows the action and invites the reader to see through the character’s eyes. In Genesis it frequently marks a moment when God’s providence becomes visible (Genesis 18:2; Genesis 22:13; Genesis 24:63). “Behold” (hinneh) signals surprise. Verse 5 repeats the first part of the formula for Esau, so that each brother in turn lifts his eyes and takes in what God has done in the other’s life.

verses.bibleText: And he put the handmaids and their children foremost, and Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph hindermost.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob sets the handmaids and their children “foremost,” Leah and her children next, and “Rachel and Joseph hindermost.” Those at the rear would be farthest from danger and closest to escape if Esau attacked. The order matches the rank of each mother in Jacob’s heart, and the narrative does not hide it. Joseph is the only child named, and his place at the back is a small sign of the partiality that will later stir his brothers’ hatred (37:3-4).

Social custom may also have shaped the procession, with the most honoured coming last before a dignitary, yet the result is the same: every member of the family could see where they stood. Genesis tells the patriarchs’ failures plainly. Jacob had suffered under a father who loved one son more than the other (25:28), and here he repeats the pattern in his own household. God’s promise is carried forward through a family that is far from ideal, which is why grace, not merit, explains its survival.

The verse warns parents and leaders that favouritism, even when it seems natural, writes itself into the memories of those who are passed over. The New Testament calls believers to honour one another without partiality (James 2:1; Romans 12:10), a standard Jacob’s household had yet to learn.

wordNotes.explanation: The plural of ’acharon, “last,” here meaning those placed at the rear of the procession. The same root supplies “after” for Leah’s group. The arrangement moves from first to last in ascending order of Jacob’s affection, and Rachel’s position recalls that Jacob had loved her more than Leah from the start (Genesis 29:30). Later, the brothers’ resentment of Joseph shows how such distinctions bore fruit (Genesis 37:4).

verses.bibleText: And he passed over before them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he passed over before them.” The day before, Jacob had sent wave after wave of gifts ahead while he stayed behind with the camp (32:16-21). Now he steps to the front, placing himself between his family and the four hundred men. The change is one of the first visible signs of Peniel. A man who had spent his life arranging others to absorb risk for him now takes the exposed place himself.

He “bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.” The verb describes full prostration, face to the earth, the posture of a subject before a king or a worshipper before God. Letters written by Canaanite princes to Pharaoh centuries later speak of falling down seven times, and seven times again, at the feet of their lord. Jacob approaches Esau with that court ceremony, bowing, rising, walking forward, and bowing again across the gap between them.

The gesture carries the weight of the past. Isaac’s stolen blessing had said, “Let people serve thee, and nations bow down to thee: be lord over thy brethren, and let thy mother’s sons bow down to thee” (27:29). Jacob had grasped at that lordship by deceit. Now the one who was to receive obeisance gives it. He does not renounce God’s purpose that the elder should serve the younger (25:23), but he lays aside any claim to rank won by fraud and comes as a penitent.

Humility of this kind is the natural fruit of an encounter with God. The man who has been brought low before the Lord finds it possible to bow before the brother he wronged. Jesus taught that the one who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11), and Peter urged believers to be clothed with humility toward one another (1 Peter 5:5).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ אַרְצָה (vayyishtachu artsah) — and bowed himself to the ground
wordNotes.explanation: The verb denotes bending low or prostrating oneself, with “to the ground” stressing the full extent of the bow. It is used of honouring a superior (Genesis 23:7; Genesis 42:6) and of worshipping God (Genesis 24:26). Context decides the sense. Here it is an act of social homage, made pointed by Isaac’s blessing that Jacob’s brothers would bow to him (Genesis 27:29). Joseph’s dreams of bowing sheaves and stars later revive the same vocabulary (Genesis 37:7).

verses.bibleText: And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Esau ran to meet him.” After twenty years of dread, after the prayers, the divided camps, the droves of goats and camels, the night of wrestling, and seven bows in the dust, the answer comes in a single rush of movement. The verbs tumble over one another: he ran, he embraced, he fell on his neck, he kissed, and they wept. When Esau once traded his birthright, the narrator described him in five curt verbs: he ate, drank, rose, went his way, and despised (25:34). Now five warm verbs describe his welcome. Jacob limps forward bowing; Esau runs.

Scripture does not explain how the murderous anger of 27:41 had turned to tenderness. Time and prosperity may have softened Esau, yet the placement of this scene directly after Jacob’s prayer (32:11) and his night with God points beyond natural causes. God had earlier restrained Laban by a warning in a dream (31:24), and here, without telling us the means, he answers the prayer of the man who had wrestled for a blessing. “When a man’s ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him” (Proverbs 16:7).

The kiss carries its own history. Jacob had kissed his father in Esau’s clothing to secure the stolen blessing (27:26-27), and the deception that divided the brothers was sealed with a kiss. Reconciliation is sealed with one too. In the traditional Hebrew text, scribes placed dots over the word “kissed,” perhaps to draw attention to it; some later readers doubted Esau’s sincerity, but the narrative offers no hint of a false embrace, and the shared tears speak for themselves.

Jesus used nearly the same words for the father in his parable who saw his son a great way off, ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him (Luke 15:20). The returning son had rehearsed his speech of unworthiness, just as Jacob had rehearsed his servant’s language, and in both cases the welcome came before the speech was finished. The scene previews the way God receives sinners who come home, and it shows what grace can do between brothers once divided by sin.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּפֹּל עַל־צַוָּארָו וַיִּשָּׁקֵהוּ (vayyippol ‘al-tsavvaro vayyishshaqehu) — and fell on his neck, and kissed him
wordNotes.explanation: To “fall on the neck” is to throw one’s arms around another in a close embrace, a gesture of overwhelming affection at reunion (Genesis 45:14; Genesis 46:29). In the Masoretic text the verb “kissed him” carries special dots over its letters, a scribal marker whose purpose is uncertain. The Greek translation of Luke 15:20 uses the matching expression for the father’s embrace of the prodigal, so the language of this reunion passes into Jesus’ portrait of the welcoming God.

verses.bibleText: And he lifted up his eyes, and saw the women and the children; and said, Who are those with thee? And he said, The children which God hath graciously given thy servant.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Now Esau lifts up his eyes, as Jacob had in verse 1, and sees the women and the children who have been drawing near during the long embrace. As the superior party he opens the conversation: “Who are those with thee?” Twenty years earlier Jacob had left with only a staff in his hand (32:10). Now he returns with four wives and eleven sons, a daughter, servants, and flocks.

Jacob’s reply is short and carefully chosen: “The children which God hath graciously given thy servant.” He speaks only of the children, saying nothing of the wives whose marriages were tied to his flight to Laban’s house. He names God as the giver, and he uses the general word Elohim rather than the covenant name, fitting language for a conversation with a brother who had stepped outside the covenant line. His word for “graciously given” belongs to the same family as “grace” and “favour” that run through the rest of the dialogue (vv. 8, 10, 15). Jacob does not boast of his increase as the fruit of his own cunning, though the account of his dealings with Laban might have tempted him to (30:37-43). He traces it to God’s free kindness.

Calling himself “thy servant” continues the posture of verse 3. In the diplomacy of the day such language marked submission to a lord. The man who had once grasped at preeminence now seeks only grace. Children are elsewhere called a heritage and reward from the Lord (Psalm 127:3), and Jacob’s answer teaches the same thankful reading of family life.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to show favour freely, to be gracious, often toward someone with no claim on it (Exodus 33:19; Psalm 51:1). Jacob uses it again in verse 11, “God hath dealt graciously with me,” and its noun chen, “grace” or “favour,” appears in verses 8, 10, and 15. The repetition binds the chapter together: Jacob has received chen from God and now seeks chen from Esau. Joseph later blesses Benjamin with the same verb (Genesis 43:29).

verses.bibleText: Then the handmaidens came near, they and their children, and they bowed themselves.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The family comes forward in the order Jacob had set. First “the handmaidens came near, they and their children, and they bowed themselves.” Bilhah and Zilpah, given to Jacob as secondary wives (30:3-4, 9), lead their four sons, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher, before the uncle they have never met. They copy the head of the household and bow to the ground.

The repetition of the verb “bowed” across verses 6 and 7 is deliberate. Each group in turn honours Esau, so that the whole household joins Jacob in acknowledging him. The homage is as public as the wrong had once been. Esau’s four hundred men and Jacob’s servants watch the patriarch’s family prostrate themselves, and the scene becomes a family confession of the debt owed to the elder brother. The sons of the handmaids would one day head tribes of Israel (49:16-21). Here, at the front of the line, they share in their father’s humility before they share in his inheritance.

wordNotes.explanation: Shifchah denotes a female servant, often a personal maid attached to her mistress, as Hagar was to Sarai (Genesis 16:1). Bilhah and Zilpah were such maids, given by Rachel and Leah to Jacob so that children born to them would be counted to their mistresses (Genesis 30:3). Their sons nonetheless received full standing among the tribes of Israel.

verses.bibleText: And Leah also with her children came near, and bowed themselves: and after came Joseph near and Rachel, and they bowed themselves.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Leah also with her children came near, and bowed themselves.” Leah brings six sons, Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun, and her daughter Dinah (30:21). From this line would come the priesthood through Levi and the kings through Judah, yet on this morning they bow in the dust before Edom’s founder.

Then “after came Joseph near and Rachel.” The order of the names is striking. Everywhere else in the procession the mother is mentioned before her children, but here Joseph stands before Rachel. Some have suggested that the boy stepped in front of his mother, perhaps to shield her; the text simply places the beloved son first. Joseph, whose dreams would one day show his brothers bowing to him (37:5-10), bows here to his uncle.

The threefold “bowed themselves” closes the presentation. Every member of Jacob’s house has now given honour to Esau, and the narrator’s careful repetition slows the moment so the reader can see a family humbled together. Reconciliation, when it comes, is rarely the work of one person alone; Jacob’s household follows where he leads.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to approach, draw near, often in a formal setting before a superior or before God (Genesis 27:21; Exodus 24:2). It appears three times in verses 6-7 for the three groups. Judah later uses the same verb when he steps forward to plead with Joseph for Benjamin’s life (Genesis 44:18), another approach to a feared ruler that ends in reconciliation.

verses.bibleText: And he said, What meanest thou by all this drove which I met? And he said, These are to find grace in the sight of my lord.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Esau’s second question concerns the flocks that had met him on the road: “What meanest thou by all this drove which I met?” The servants had delivered Jacob’s message with each drove (32:17-19), so Esau knows what was said; his question invites Jacob to state his purpose face to face. The word “drove” is literally “camp,” the same term Jacob used for his two companies (32:7) and for the angelic host he named at Mahanaim (32:2). Jacob’s real “army” against Esau turned out to be a procession of gifts.

Jacob answers plainly: “These are to find grace in the sight of my lord.” A man who once gained his ends by disguise now states his motive without pretence. He wants Esau’s favour, his acceptance and forgiveness, and he says so. The phrase “find grace in the sight of” is the language of a petitioner before someone with power to grant or refuse (6:8; 39:4), and Jacob uses it three times in this chapter (vv. 8, 10, 15).

The answer also carries a lesson about the order of grace. Jacob had sent the gifts hoping to appease Esau (32:20), yet Esau had already embraced him before the matter of the gifts came up. The gift could no longer win a forgiveness already given; it could only express gratitude and seal the peace.

wordNotes.explanation: Usually “camp” or “company,” whether of travelers, soldiers, or angels (Genesis 32:2; Exodus 14:19). Here it describes the successive droves of livestock Jacob sent ahead. The word sounds like minchah, “present,” in verse 10 and chen, “grace,” in the same sentence, so the dialogue keeps camp, gift, and grace ringing together. Mahanaim, “two camps,” had marked God’s host meeting Jacob on the way (Genesis 32:2).

verses.bibleText: And Esau said, I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself.” Esau’s refusal is courteous and probably sincere. Ancient etiquette expected a first refusal of a gift (compare Ephron’s offer in 23:11), but Esau had no need of Jacob’s animals. Isaac’s words to him had promised a life by the sword in a land away from the fatness of the earth (27:39-40), and he had prospered as a chieftain in Seir. He commands four hundred men and lacks nothing.

The forms of address are revealing. Jacob has called Esau “my lord” and himself “thy servant” (vv. 5, 8). Esau answers with “my brother.” The elder offers kinship; the younger keeps his distance with the language of diplomacy. Esau may simply be warmer, Jacob more wary, yet the contrast also shows Jacob’s determination not to presume on the relationship he had once broken.

Notice, too, what Esau does not say. He speaks of having “enough,” but he does not name God as its source, while Jacob will say that he has enough “because God hath dealt graciously with me” (v. 11). Both men are rich; only one is thankful to God. Esau’s generosity is real and admirable, and Scripture does not belittle it. Still, Hebrews remembers him as one who sold his birthright for a meal and later could not reverse the loss (Hebrews 12:16-17). A forgiving spirit toward a brother is a fine thing, and it does not replace faith in the God of the promise.

wordNotes.term: יֶשׁ־לִי רָב (yesh-li rav) — I have enough
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “there is to me much.” Rav means much or abundant. In verse 11 Jacob answers with a different word, kol, “I have all” or “I have everything” (yesh-li khol). Esau has plenty; Jacob claims to have all he needs. The two phrases sit side by side, and only Jacob links his sufficiency to God. Paul later describes the contentment of having all things in Christ (Philippians 4:18).

verses.bibleText: And Jacob said, Nay, I pray thee, if now I have found grace in thy sight, then receive my present at my hand: for therefore I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God, and thou wast pleased with me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Nay, I pray thee.” Jacob will not take Esau’s refusal. The man who had held on at Peniel until he was blessed (32:26) now holds on until his gift is received. His reason is set in a careful sequence: if he has found grace, then Esau should receive his present, because seeing Esau’s face has been like seeing the face of God, and Esau has been pleased with him. Acceptance of the gift would be the outward seal of a peace already granted. In that culture a superior who received a present thereby accepted the giver and bound himself to friendship; a refused gift left the relationship uncertain.

“For therefore I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God.” The words reach back over a single night. Jacob had planned the gifts in hope that he might see Esau’s face and be accepted (32:20). Then he wrestled with the One whose face he saw, naming the place Peniel because “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved” (32:30). The Angel he met there was no created messenger. Hosea calls him God and the Angel in the same breath (Hosea 12:3-5), and he is best understood as the pre-incarnate Christ. Jacob had faced the One whose holiness might have destroyed him, and his life had been spared. Now he faces the brother whose anger might have killed him, and again he is received.

The comparison does not make Esau divine, nor is it empty flattery. Jacob recognizes in Esau’s welcome the same mercy he met at the Jabbok. The God who blessed him at night has gone before him by day, and the softened face of his brother is evidence of God’s hand. Grace from God had made grace from Esau possible.

“And thou wast pleased with me” uses a verb that elsewhere describes God accepting a worshipper and his offering (Leviticus 1:4; Malachi 1:10). The gift is like a tribute brought before one who has graciously received the giver. Jesus would teach that a gift brought to the altar is hollow while a brother still has something against us (Matthew 5:23-24), and John asks how anyone can love the unseen God while hating the brother he sees (1 John 4:20). In Jacob’s experience, reconciliation with God and reconciliation with his brother came on successive days, and each shed light on the other. Through Christ, God reconciles sinners to himself and then entrusts them with the ministry of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18-20).

wordNotes.term: כִּרְאֹת פְּנֵי אֱלֹהִים (kir’ot pene ’Elohim) — as though I had seen the face of God
wordNotes.explanation: Pene ’Elohim, “the face of God,” deliberately echoes Peniel, “face of God” (Genesis 32:30), where Jacob saw God and lived. To see the face of a king could mean being admitted to his favour (2 Samuel 14:24), and to see God’s face without dying was a mark of extraordinary mercy (Exodus 33:20; Judges 13:22). The comparative “as though” keeps the distinction clear: Esau is not God, yet his gracious welcome mirrors the divine acceptance Jacob had just received.

wordNotes.term: וַתִּרְצֵנִי (vattirtseni) — and thou wast pleased with me
wordNotes.explanation: From ratsah, “to be pleased with, accept favourably.” The verb and its noun ratson are common in sacrificial texts for God’s acceptance of an offering and the one who brings it (Leviticus 1:4; Leviticus 22:27; Malachi 1:10). Jacob’s choice of word frames his present as a tribute laid before one who has already graciously accepted him. Psalm 147:11 speaks of the Lord taking pleasure in those who hope in his mercy.

verses.bibleText: Take, I pray thee, my blessing that is brought to thee; because God hath dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough. And he urged him, and he took it.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Take, I pray thee, my blessing that is brought to thee.” Until now Jacob has called his gift a minchah, a present or tribute (32:13, 18, 20; 33:10). Here he changes the word to berakhah, “blessing.” It is the very word used for what he stole when he deceived his father, and Esau’s bitter cry still echoes from that day: “He took away my birthright; and, behold, now he hath taken away my blessing” (27:36). Neither brother names the old wrong, yet the word does the work. Jacob cannot hand back Isaac’s spoken blessing, which God had confirmed and would not revoke (27:33; 28:3-4). He can share the material fruit of the blessing with the brother he cheated, and he does so as a token of restitution.

His reasons are twofold: “because God hath dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough.” The first credits God with all his wealth, the second declares his contentment. Literally Jacob says “I have everything,” a step beyond Esau’s “I have plenty” (v. 9). The man who once took what was not his now gives freely because he has received freely. Grace from God had made a grasping man generous.

“And he urged him, and he took it.” The verb for urging is the same used when Lot pressed the angels to lodge in his house (19:3); Jacob presses until Esau relents. Esau gives nothing back in exchange, which in that setting signified that he received the gift as settlement of the wrong done to him. His acceptance, witnessed by both households, sealed the reconciliation as surely as a signed agreement.

Restitution belongs to genuine repentance throughout Scripture. The law required the one who wronged a neighbour to restore what was taken and add to it (Leviticus 6:4-5), and Zacchaeus, once Jesus entered his house, offered fourfold to any he had defrauded (Luke 19:8). Such giving does not purchase God’s pardon. It flows from a heart that has already met mercy and wants to make right, as far as possible, what sin has damaged.

wordNotes.explanation: Berakhah usually means a spoken blessing, but it can also denote a gift that expresses goodwill (1 Samuel 25:27; 2 Kings 5:15). The shift from minchah in verse 10 to berakhah here is pointed, since berakhah is the word for what Jacob took from Esau (Genesis 27:35-36). By offering “my blessing,” Jacob makes a costly gesture of restitution without reopening the past in words.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Let us take our journey, and let us go, and I will go before thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having accepted the gift, Esau proposes that the brothers travel together: “Let us take our journey, and let us go, and I will go before thee.” Jacob’s messengers had announced his coming to Esau in Seir (32:3-5), so Esau naturally assumes that Seir is Jacob’s goal. His offer to lead is the gesture of a host escorting an honoured guest, and it confirms that his forgiveness is complete. The brother who once vowed to kill Jacob now volunteers to protect him on the road.

Yet the offer creates a new problem. Seir lay outside the land God had promised, and Jacob had been told to return “unto the land of thy fathers, and to thy kindred” (31:3). His vow at Bethel looked toward coming back to his father’s house in peace (28:21). To follow Esau south would turn the pilgrim away from the place God had appointed. The kindness of a reconciled brother could become a quiet detour from God’s purpose.

The chapter thus moves from fear of Esau’s hostility to the subtler test of his friendship. Peace with others is a gift to be treasured, but it does not settle the question of where God is leading. Abraham and Lot had found that two large households could not share one pasture (13:6), and the same practical truth will soon be stated of Jacob and Esau (36:6-7).

wordNotes.term: נִסְעָה וְנֵלֵכָה (nis‘ah venelekhah) — let us take our journey, and let us go
wordNotes.explanation: Two first-person plural verbs in the form of an urging: “let us set out and let us go.” Nasa‘ originally meant pulling up tent pegs to break camp, and it is the standard verb for stages of a journey (Genesis 12:9; Numbers 10:12). Esau pictures the two companies moving as one. Verse 17 uses the same verb for Jacob alone, journeying not to Seir but to Succoth.

verses.bibleText: And he said unto him, My lord knoweth that the children are tender, and the flocks and herds with young are with me: and if men should overdrive them one day, all the flock will die.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob declines with a shepherd’s reasoning: “My lord knoweth that the children are tender, and the flocks and herds with young are with me: and if men should overdrive them one day, all the flock will die.” His youngest children were small; Joseph could have been no more than about six. Ewes and cows nursing their young cannot be hurried over rough ground without loss. A war band of four hundred men moved at a pace that would have destroyed Jacob’s animals within days.

The explanation is true in every detail. Jacob had spent twenty years as a herdsman, and he had told Laban how he bore the heat by day and the frost by night for the flock’s sake (31:38-40). He knew what overdriving does to pregnant and nursing animals. His reply shows a man who still thinks like a careful shepherd, moving at the pace of the weakest in his charge.

That picture reaches forward to God’s own care for his people. Isaiah describes the Lord gathering the lambs in his arm and gently leading those that are with young (Isaiah 40:11), and Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who knows his sheep (John 10:11, 14). Leaders among God’s people are likewise told to shepherd the flock willingly, as examples rather than taskmasters (1 Peter 5:2-3). Jacob’s concern for the tender ones, whatever else lay behind his refusal, is one of the most attractive things about him.

wordNotes.explanation: Rakh describes what is soft, delicate, or young and vulnerable. It is used of a tender calf (Genesis 18:7), of young Solomon as inexperienced (1 Chronicles 29:1), and of a gentle answer (Proverbs 15:1). Here it marks the children as too young and frail for a forced march. Jacob’s concern rests on their weakness, not on any wish to keep his brother at a distance.

verses.bibleText: Let my lord, I pray thee, pass over before his servant: and I will lead on softly, according as the cattle that goeth before me and the children be able to endure, until I come unto my lord unto Seir.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Let my lord, I pray thee, pass over before his servant: and I will lead on softly, according as the cattle that goeth before me and the children be able to endure, until I come unto my lord unto Seir.” Jacob asks Esau to go on ahead while he follows at the pace his animals and children can bear. The phrase “lead on softly” pictures a slow, gentle walk, letting the weakest set the speed.

The words “until I come unto my lord unto Seir” raise a question, for verse 17 sends Jacob north to Succoth and then west to Shechem. Was Jacob deceiving his brother again? The narrator who openly said that Jacob “stole away unawares” from Laban (31:20) passes no such verdict here. Jacob may well have meant to visit Seir at some later time, once his household was settled in Canaan; the Hebrew does not say he would follow at once. The brothers did meet again as friends when they buried their father (35:29), and Esau’s later move away from Jacob’s country suggests continued goodwill (36:6-8). Scripture does not record whether a visit ever took place.

Still, the reader cannot miss that Jacob’s polite words leave his true plans unspoken. Courtesy may have kept him from saying outright that he would not live near Esau, and both men may have understood the convention. The narrative lets that tension stand without excusing or condemning it, and the honest reader can learn from it. The God who had renamed Jacob calls his people to let their yes be yes and their no be no (Matthew 5:37), and to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15). Wise separation does not require vague promises, and the new Israel was still learning to walk as straight as he now limped.

What is clear is Jacob’s commitment to the land of promise. Whatever his intentions toward Seir, he would not allow even a reconciled brother to draw him away from the place where God had sent him.

wordNotes.term: אֶתְנָהֲלָה לְאִטִּי (’etnahalah le’itti) — I will lead on softly
wordNotes.explanation: Nahal means to lead or guide to a resting place, often with the idea of gentle care; in Isaiah 40:11 the Lord “gently leads” the nursing ewes, and Psalm 23:2 speaks of being led beside still waters. Le’itti, “at my gentle pace,” stresses slowness. Together the words picture a shepherd matching his stride to the weakest of his flock.

Seir is the mountainous region south of the Dead Sea, later called Edom, where Esau had settled (Genesis 32:3; Genesis 36:8). The name sounds like sa‘ir, “hairy,” recalling Esau’s appearance at birth (Genesis 25:25). It lay outside the land promised to Abraham’s line through Isaac, and Moses later reminded Israel that God had given Mount Seir to Esau as his possession (Deuteronomy 2:5).

verses.bibleText: And Esau said, Let me now leave with thee some of the folk that are with me. And he said, What needeth it? let me find grace in the sight of my lord.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Esau makes a second offer: “Let me now leave with you some of the folk that are with me.” If Jacob will not travel with him, he can at least have an escort for protection on the roads. The offer is generous and practical. Bands of raiders were a real threat in the region, and a company of armed men would discourage attack.

Jacob again declines: “What needeth it? let me find grace in the sight of my lord.” He has no need of a human guard. The day before, he had seen the camp of God’s angels meeting him on the way (32:1-2), and he had just been told that he had prevailed with God and with men (32:28). The armed men who had approached as a threat would add nothing to the protection God was already giving. There may also have been wisdom in avoiding obligation to Esau’s men, who would watch his household and report back to Seir.

His final words, “let me find grace in the sight of my lord,” close the dialogue on the note that has run through it. Jacob does not argue; he simply asks his brother to grant him this kindness too. The phrase works as a courteous way of declining, a request that Esau not press the matter. It is the fifth exchange between the brothers, and every one of Jacob’s answers has turned on grace: grace from God in his children and his wealth, grace from Esau in his welcome.

wordNotes.term: לָמָּה זֶּה (lammah zeh) — What needeth it?
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “why this?” The phrase questions the need for something without hostility, as when Rebekah asked why her pregnancy was so troubled (Genesis 25:22). Ezra later declined a royal escort because he had told the king that God’s hand was on those who seek him (Ezra 8:22). Jacob’s refusal rests on a similar confidence in divine protection.

verses.bibleText: So Esau returned that day on his way unto Seir.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“So Esau returned that day on his way unto Seir.” The verse is brief, and its brevity is part of its meaning. The four hundred men who had filled Jacob’s thoughts for a day and a night turn south and disappear down the road. The threat that hung over the story since chapter 27 dissolves without a blow struck.

Esau “returned,” going back to a place already his own. The Hebrew sentence places the verb first for Esau, and verse 17 places Jacob’s name first, setting the two departures side by side: Esau went back, but Jacob journeyed on. They would never again live in the same region (36:6-7), and apart from the burial of their father (35:29) Esau steps out of the main story of salvation. His descendants are listed in chapter 36, and the long history between Edom and Israel would include both kinship and conflict (Numbers 20:14-21; Obadiah 1:10-12).

The peaceful parting fulfils Jacob’s prayer for deliverance from Esau’s hand (32:11). Brothers who could not live together could still part as friends, and that was itself a mercy.

wordNotes.explanation: From shuv, “to turn back, return,” the ordinary verb for going home or reversing direction. Its use here implies a fixed starting point: Esau goes back to the territory he already holds. The same verb runs through Jacob’s story for his return to the land (Genesis 28:15; Genesis 31:3), but Jacob’s homecoming points to Canaan while Esau’s points to Seir.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built him an house, and made booths for his cattle: therefore the name of the place is called Succoth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob journeyed to Succoth.” Instead of turning south toward Seir, Jacob crosses back over the Jabbok and settles in the Jordan Valley, a short distance east of the river. Succoth would later be allotted to Gad (Joshua 13:27), and Gideon would pass through it in pursuit of the Midianites (Judges 8:5). The region offered water and pasture for a large herd.

He “built him an house, and made booths for his cattle.” This is the first time a patriarch is said to have built a house. Abraham and Isaac lived in tents throughout their sojourning (Hebrews 11:9), and the building of a house suggests that Jacob stayed for some time, perhaps several years. The animals, many of them weakened by the journey and nursing young, were given shelters of woven branches. The place took its name from these: Succoth means “booths.”

The name holds a deeper resonance for later readers. Israel would one day live in booths in the wilderness after leaving Egypt, and the Feast of Tabernacles kept that memory alive (Leviticus 23:42-43). A booth is a temporary shelter, a fitting image for a pilgrim people who are not yet at rest. Jacob was still east of the Jordan, outside Canaan proper, and the narrative does not say why he lingered. Good pasture may have drawn him, or the needs of the young animals he had spoken of to Esau.

Yet Bethel, where he had vowed to return, lay ahead (28:20-22). A house at Succoth, comfortable as it was, was not the house of God. The pause is understandable, and it also hints at a recurring danger for those whom God has brought through a crisis: to settle down short of the place to which he has called them.

wordNotes.explanation: The plural of sukkah, a temporary shelter made of branches or leafy boughs, used for animals, soldiers in the field, or a watchman (2 Samuel 11:11; Jonah 4:5). The town is named for the shelters Jacob made. The same word names the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel lived in booths to remember God’s care in the wilderness (Leviticus 23:42-43). The Succoth of Jacob’s story is a different place from the Succoth on the Exodus route (Exodus 12:37).

verses.bibleText: And Jacob came to Shalem, a city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Padan-aram; and pitched his tent before the city.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob came to Shalem, a city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Padan-aram.” With this sentence Jacob crosses the Jordan and stands again in the land of promise. The narrator underlines it: the place is “in the land of Canaan,” and he has come “from Padan-aram.” The long exile that began at Beersheba (28:10) is over.

The word the KJV reads as a place name, Shalem, is more likely an adverb meaning “safely,” “in peace,” or “whole.” The early Greek and Latin versions treated it as a town, and a village called Salim lies near Shechem today, yet the sense “Jacob came in peace to the city of Shechem” fits the story better. Twenty years earlier at Bethel, Jacob had vowed that if God would keep him on his way and bring him back to his father’s house “in peace,” the LORD would be his God (28:20-21). The same root is used here. God had kept every part of his word: he had been with Jacob, protected him from Laban and from Esau, and brought him home whole, though limping.

Shechem itself was rich in memory. It was the first place Abram stopped in Canaan, where the LORD appeared to him and promised the land to his seed, and where he built his first altar (12:6-7). Jacob “pitched his tent before the city,” camping on its outskirts rather than moving within its walls. The tent recalls the pilgrim life of his fathers (Hebrews 11:9).

Yet Shechem was not Bethel. The vow had named Bethel as the place where God’s house would be, and Jacob stops some twenty miles short of it. The next chapter will show the cost of settling beside a Canaanite city, and in chapter 35 God himself will tell Jacob to rise and go up to Bethel. For now, the verse celebrates a promise kept. God’s faithfulness ran ahead of Jacob’s, and the peace in which he arrived was entirely God’s gift (Psalm 121:7-8).

wordNotes.explanation: An adjective meaning whole, complete, sound, or at peace, related to shalom. Used adverbially it describes arriving safe and unharmed. The KJV, following the Septuagint and Vulgate, took it as a town name, but the link with Jacob’s vow, “so that I come again to my father’s house in peace” (beshalom, Genesis 28:21), strongly suggests the meaning “safely.” The word also describes a heart wholly devoted to God (1 Kings 8:61).

verses.bibleText: And he bought a parcel of a field, where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem's father, for an hundred pieces of money.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he bought a parcel of a field, where he had spread his tent.” Jacob becomes only the second patriarch to own land in Canaan. Abraham had bought the field and cave of Machpelah as a burial place for Sarah (23:16-20); Jacob buys ground for living and worship. He purchases it “at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem’s father,” naming the family who will dominate the next chapter. Hamor was the local ruler, and his son Shechem bore the name of the city.

The price was “an hundred pieces of money.” The Hebrew unit, qesitah, appears only here, in Joshua 24:32, and in Job 42:11. Its value is unknown, and the Greek translation renders it “a hundred lambs,” perhaps because early money was sometimes reckoned by livestock or bore an animal’s image. The purchase was a legal transaction, done openly, and it gave Jacob a lawful claim to that ground.

The act was also a statement of faith. God had promised the whole land to Jacob’s seed (28:13), yet Jacob owned none of it. By buying a field, he planted his household in Canaan as heir of the promise, much as Jeremiah would later buy a field at Anathoth as a sign that God would restore the land (Jeremiah 32:9-15). This field became a lasting family possession. Jacob bequeathed it to Joseph (48:22), and centuries later the Israelites buried Joseph’s bones there, fulfilling his dying request (Joshua 24:32; Genesis 50:25). Stephen, compressing the patriarchal burials, recalls the tomb bought from the sons of Hamor at Shechem (Acts 7:16).

Near this ground stood the well known as Jacob’s. Two thousand years later Jesus, tired from travel, sat by it and offered a Samaritan woman living water that would spring up into everlasting life (John 4:5-14). The field Jacob purchased in faith became the setting where the promised Seed revealed himself as the Messiah.

wordNotes.explanation: A unit of value found only in Genesis 33:19, Joshua 24:32, and Job 42:11, where Job’s friends each give him one. Its weight or worth is unknown. The Septuagint translates it “lambs,” which may preserve a memory of value measured in livestock. The rare word suggests an early setting and disappears from later Hebrew, where the shekel became the usual measure (Genesis 23:16).

verses.bibleText: And he erected there an altar, and called it El-elohe-Israel.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he erected there an altar, and called it El-elohe-Israel.” The first thing Jacob does on his own land is set up a place of worship. Abraham had done the same at Shechem when he first entered Canaan (12:7), and Jacob likely chose the site with that earlier altar in mind. Whatever else the purchase of land meant, it was ground on which to call on the name of the Lord.

The verb is unusual. Altars are normally “built,” but here Jacob “erected” or “set up” the altar, using the verb that describes setting up a standing stone or pillar (28:18; 35:14, 20). The choice links this act to Bethel, where he had set up a stone as a pillar and anointed it. The structure at Shechem may have served as both altar and memorial, a marker declaring to all who passed whose land this was and whose God was worshipped there.

The name says everything. El-elohe-Israel means “God, the God of Israel,” or “mighty is the God of Israel.” El is the ancient name for God in his strength, the Creator and Most High (14:19). Israel is Jacob’s new name, given at Peniel only days before (32:28). Until now Jacob had spoken of “the God of my father” and “the God of Abraham, and the Fear of Isaac” (31:5, 42). Here, for the first time, he names God in relation to himself under his new name. At Bethel he had said, “then shall the LORD be my God” (28:21), and the altar confesses that this condition has been met. The God of his fathers has become his own God.

The name also looks forward. Israel would become the name of a nation, and generations later Joshua gathered that nation at Shechem to renew the covenant with the God of Israel (Joshua 24:1, 25-26). Jesus, standing near the same place, would tell a Samaritan woman that the Father seeks those who worship him in spirit and in truth (John 4:20-24). Personal faith in the God who saves, offered in grateful worship, is the true end of every journey God directs.

The chapter closes on a high note, yet the story does not stop here. Shechem was a stopping place on the way to Bethel, not a substitute for it, and the next chapters will show both the dangers of lingering and God’s patient call to finish what had been vowed. Even so, the altar stands as a confession made in faith: the God who met Jacob as a fugitive, wrestled with him as a stranger, and brought him home in peace is the mighty God of Israel.

wordNotes.explanation: A name meaning “God, the God of Israel.” ’El is the common Semitic word for God, often stressing might and supremacy (Genesis 14:19; Psalm 50:1); ’elohe means “God of.” Some read the first word as the preposition ’el, giving “to the God of Israel,” yet the traditional reading treats it as a confession. The pattern resembles El-bethel in Genesis 35:7. Jacob’s new name stands in the confession, and “the God of Israel” later becomes a standard title for the Lord (Exodus 5:1).

The Hiphil of natsav, “to set up, station, erect.” It is used for setting up pillars and memorial stones (Genesis 35:14; Genesis 35:20) rather than the usual verb for building an altar (Genesis 12:7, banah). Its noun matsevah names the pillar Jacob set up at Bethel (Genesis 28:18). The verb may hint that the altar doubled as a memorial marking God’s faithfulness.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What would it take for you to walk toward someone you once wronged, not knowing how they would receive you?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The God who met Jacob at Peniel went before him to Esau, turning a feared confrontation into an embrace, and Jacob responded with humility, restitution, gratitude, and worship.
discussionQuestions: Why does Jacob now walk in front of his family instead of behind it, and what had changed overnight?
What does Jacob’s use of “my blessing” in verse 11 suggest about how he understood his gift?
Why would Jacob compare his brother’s welcoming face with the face he saw at Peniel, and what does that comparison teach about grace?
Was Jacob right to decline traveling with Esau, and what do you make of his words about coming to Seir?
What does the altar named El-elohe-Israel reveal about Jacob’s faith at the end of his journey home?
commonMisunderstandings: Jacob’s bowing and gifts did not buy Esau’s forgiveness; Esau ran to him before any word was spoken, and the change in Esau answered Jacob’s prayer (32:11).
Verse 10 does not make Esau divine; Jacob sees in his brother’s welcome the same mercy he had met at Peniel.
Reconciliation does not require living together; the brothers part in peace and meet again as friends at their father’s burial (35:29).
The altar at Shechem does not mean Jacob’s pilgrimage was complete; his vow at Bethel still waited, and God would call him there (35:1).
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the order of the story: God met Jacob first, then went before him to Esau. Humility and restitution follow grace and do not earn it, and the chapter closes with worship.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Take the step toward the brother or sister you have wronged, trusting the God who has already met you and who can go before you, and give him the praise when peace comes.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Reconciliation with God and with others: God reconciles sinners to himself through Christ and sends them, humbled and forgiven, to make peace with those they have wronged.
flow: Jacob had wronged his brother and lived for twenty years under the shadow of that sin.
Before meeting Esau, Jacob met God at Peniel and came away broken, blessed, and renamed.
God went before him, and the brother he feared ran to embrace him.
Like the father in Jesus’ parable, God runs to welcome the returning sinner through Christ.
Those who have been received by God are called to seek peace with others and to worship the God who made them his own.
simpleIllustrations: A man rehearses a long apology on the drive to his estranged brother’s house, only to find the door flung open before he reaches the step; the rehearsed speech still matters, but the welcome was given first.

A traveler who has been away for years plants a garden as soon as he comes home; Jacob’s purchase of land and his altar said in the same way, “This is where God has brought me, and here I stay to worship.”
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Having been met by God’s mercy in Christ, will you let him send you to make peace with the one you have wronged?
cautions: Do not teach that restitution earns God’s forgiveness; it is the fruit of a heart already met by grace.
Do not press reconciliation in ways that ignore real danger or abuse; Jacob sought peace with wisdom and kept a prudent distance.
Do not present Esau as an example of saving faith; his warmth is admirable, yet Scripture elsewhere warns against his profane disregard for the birthright (Hebrews 12:16-17).

reflectionQuestions: Whom have I wronged that I have avoided facing, and what keeps me from walking toward them?
Do I see the hand of God when someone receives me with mercy I did not deserve?
Am I willing to give back something costly as a sign that I am sorry, without expecting it to earn forgiveness?
Where have I stopped short of a promise I made to God, settling comfortably on the way?
Can I say of the God of my parents that he is now my God, the God of my own life?
